description: We are a team of five passionate technology enthusiasts from Vivekananda Institute of Professional Studies (VIPS), driven by innovation and a shared interest in space technology, AI and machine learning.
summary: Our 5 member team from Vivekananda Institute of Professional Studies (VIPS-TC) presents AETHRA, an AI powered Earth monitoring and environmental intelligence platform. Current NASA Earthdata satellites record immense daily amounts of heat, rainfall, soil moisture, vegetation, groundwater etc. However, researchers and local planners find it difficult to comprehend how these different elements interact.  We have included eight satellite missions into a simple interactive map and cloud Python machine learning engine in order to address the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Users can access three distinct scientific outputs by simply clicking on any coordinate on Earth to receive real-time data from NASA POWER: 1) Scikit An observed statistical anomaly score is provided by Learn Isolation Forest.2) A composite environmental risk index ranging from zero to one hundred is provided.3) Holt exponential smoothing for a 30-day temperature forecast. Using AETHRA as decision support, complicated satellite records are made easy and actionable through transparent feature attribution and instantaneous spreadsheet/snapshot exports
details:
What AETHRA Does and How It Works

A common limitation across many climate and environment monitoring sites is that they show individual metrics in isolation: temperature, fire risk etc. Each site requires some mental effort to put together an overall picture. AETHRA removes this need. Powered by a cloud-hosted ML service, AETHRA aggregates various NASA Earth data products to display current values of land surface temperature, root-zone soil moisture, groundwater, NDVI and number of active fires. These have been summarized into 3 key messages: Observe, Understand and Anticipate.

To use AETHRA, click any point on the world map, or select one of our 5 fixed study locations (Delhi, Manaus, Fresno-Central Valley, Nairobi, Svalbard). Data is pulled via the NASA POWER endpoint (last 30 days of daily records), and additional satellite data is combined from NASA Worldview and GIBS. After computation on our server, we return 3 distinct metrics that others conflate, and so we wanted to ensure are kept clearly demarcated:

A measurable shift from the average. “How unusual is it to see these conditions today?” Our method uses an Isolation Forest model (scikit-learn) and Z-scores compared to a 30 year historical baseline. Results are shown in sigma.

Environmental Risk Index. “Given what we’re seeing, how concerning is this?” Based on a fitted logit function incorporating the effects of elevated temperatures, drier soils (SMAP), declining aquifers (GRACE-FO) and increased active fire events (FIRMS), AETHRA returns a value between 0 and 100.

Outlook for the coming 30 days. “What can we expect over the next month?” Using Holt’s Double Exponential Smoother across the previous 30-day record, we forecast the following 30 days, returning the forecast with an associated uncertainty range.

Why We Feel It Will Be Valuable:

AETHRA doesn’t shout. At its most basic level, users are presented with a central satellite based map view, a horizontal list of suggested key areas of interest, and an ‘Inspector’ panel (similar to e.g. Google Maps).

But it can be expanded. Once the user turns on Advanced Filters, AETHRA expands the page to reveal a set of tools used for formal analysis. Users can vary the input parameters (4 sliders for temp, rainfall, soil moisture, NDVI); inspect the past record alongside the 30-day outlook; review the contribution of each variable to the output (SHAP plot); compare the scene before vs after; and ask AETHRA free-text questions.

Finally, users can export their findings. Under the Export dropdown, a user can generate a large image file capturing their selected AOI, an Excel file containing multiple relevant worksheets, or a .md summary. All of these formats are readily compatible with downstream workflows.

Technical Implementation:

Frontend (hosted on GitHub Pages): Semantic HTML structure comprising 5 static pages (Home, Dashboard, Source Code, About, Contact); bespoke CSS integrated with Tailwind; JS modules. The map is implemented using Leaflet and Esri World Imagery, augmented by dynamic NASA GIBS feeds. Time-series plots and SHAP are rendered by Chart.js. The Excel exports are created client-side with SheetJS.

Backend (hosted on Render): Implemented in Python 3.11, leveraging FastAPI and Uvicorn. Dependent packages include numpy, pydantic, scikit-learn. For the Ask AETHRA feature, we call 2 open-source SLMs (llama-3.3-70b-versatile, qwen/qwen3-32b) using the native GroqCloud library.

Rationale for Approach:

Our group studies at Vivekananda Institute of Professional Studies (VIPS), and developed AETHRA around the following considerations:

1) Make it accessible to non-specialists. Many existing platforms require significant onboarding before even attempting simple tasks. By separating the ‘standard’ and ‘advanced’ functionality, we aimed to provide a common interface for both members of the general public and specialist practitioners.

2) Ensure robustness. Cloud offerings on no-cost tiers are liable to shut down at any point, and users may experience poor connectivity. As a result, we designed AETHRA to run the required calculations locally on the user’s device, ensuring an uninterrupted flow of data.

3) Follow best practice for display of NASA data. Our project relied entirely on publicly available scientific datasets and imagery, and we took care not to incorporate NASA branded assets or imagery in our deliverables.
